title: Molecular Clocks
objectives: Explain how calibrated molecular change can estimate divergence times.
Calculate time in a clearly stated simplified rate model.
Evaluate rate variation, saturation and calibration uncertainty.

glossary.definition: A model that relates genetic change to elapsed evolutionary time.
Use of independent evidence to constrain the relationship between change and time.
A condition in which repeated changes obscure some earlier substitutions at observed positions.

slides.title: A relationship between change and time
slides.html: A molecular clock uses the accumulation of molecular differences to estimate the timing of evolutionary events. It is a statistical model, not a literal biological stopwatch. The method requires a suitable sequence comparison and assumptions about change rates. Greater observed difference can suggest greater elapsed time, but it does not supply a date by itself.

slides.title: Calibration provides the time scale
slides.html: Independent evidence such as appropriately interpreted fossils can constrain dates for nodes or lineages. These constraints help estimate a molecular change rate. The relevant fossil must be assigned to the correct group, and a fossil often supplies a minimum age rather than the exact time of the common ancestor. Calibration uncertainty affects the final estimate.

diagram.caption: Illustrative times only, not dates for real taxa. Independent age constraints anchor the molecular model to a time scale.

slides.title: Distinguish one lineage from two
slides.html: Differences between two modern lineages can include changes accumulated along both branches since their common ancestor. In a simplified equal-rate model, pairwise divergence D = 2rt, where r is the per-lineage rate. If a question instead supplies an already combined pairwise rate, do not multiply it by two again.

slides.title: Worked example: a pairwise rate
slides.html: A hypothetical aligned marker differs by 6% between two lineages. Suppose the calibrated combined pairwise rate is 1.5 percentage points per million years. Then t = 6/1.5 = 4 million years. This calculation assumes the provided linear model applies; the observed percentage is not automatically a raw count of every historical substitution.

slides.title: Rates are not universally constant
slides.html: Different genes, genomic regions and lineages can evolve at different rates. Functional constraints, generation times and other factors can influence patterns. Modern analyses can allow rate variation rather than assuming one strict clock everywhere. Using a calibration from an unsuitable region or lineage can give an unjustified date.

slides.title: Repeated changes hide history
slides.html: A site might change from A to G and later back to A. Comparing only the final sequences would not reveal both events. At deeper divergences, repeated substitutions can therefore make observed differences underestimate historical change. This saturation problem means an uncorrected linear difference count can become misleading.

diagram.caption: Identical endpoints do not establish no change: a hypothetical site could follow A → G → A between observations. The sequences shown are endpoints, not a complete mutation record.

slides.title: Recent events can also be difficult
slides.html: Very recent lineages may differ at few sites, making estimates sensitive to sampling and stochastic variation. Existing ancestral variation can persist across a split, so the time when gene copies share an ancestor need not exactly equal the population or species divergence time. More sequences do not remove the need for an appropriate model.

slides.title: Report estimates with uncertainty
slides.html: A good clock analysis states the markers, calibration assumptions, rate model and uncertainty interval. Conflicting estimates from different markers should be investigated rather than averaged without thought. Molecular dates are strengthened by agreement with independently interpreted fossils and other evidence, while uncertainty should remain visible in the conclusion.

slides.title: A clock needs a measured quantity
slides.html: A molecular clock starts with differences in an appropriately aligned marker and relates them to time through a rate model. Counting endpoint differences is an observation; converting that count into a date is an inference. The two should not be collapsed. A marker can provide useful relationship information even when its rate is too uncertain to justify a precise divergence date.

slides.title: Track the units before calculating
slides.html: A supplied rate of two percentage points of pairwise difference per million years means that a six-percentage-point difference corresponds to 6 ÷ 2 = 3 million years in that model. A rate stated per lineage describes only one accumulating branch. If the branches are assumed equal, combine their contributions before converting the pairwise difference. This avoids a factor-of-two error.

slides.title: One elapsed time, two accumulating lineages
Why calibration is not perfect
slides.html: A fossil can establish that a lineage existed by a certain time, but it rarely records the exact instant two lineages separated. Its anatomical assignment and geological date also have uncertainty. Consequently, using it as a calibration involves an interpreted constraint, not a flawless timestamp. An estimate should retain uncertainty introduced by the independent evidence used to place its time scale.

slides.title: An observed match can hide change
slides.html: Imagine a lineage changing at one position from A to G and later from G back to A. A comparison with an unchanged A lineage would show no endpoint difference at that site despite two historical substitutions. Other repeated changes can also be hidden. Raw sequence differences can therefore underestimate accumulated change, particularly when enough time has passed for sites to be altered repeatedly.

slides.title: Functional constraints influence rates
slides.html: A change that disrupts an important protein function may reduce reproductive success and be removed by selection more often than a tolerated change elsewhere. Different parts of a sequence can consequently show different patterns of preserved variation. A rate estimated from one region should not be transferred automatically to another region with different constraints. A clock model must match the kind of molecular evidence being analysed.

slides.title: Calibration uncertainty affects a clock estimate
A worked sensitivity comparison
slides.html: Suppose an invented pairwise divergence is eight percentage points. A combined rate of two percentage points per million years gives four million years; a rate of one gives eight million years. The observed data have not changed, but the inference has. Showing both calculations makes the dependence on calibration explicit and demonstrates why an exact date cannot be justified by the difference percentage alone.

slides.title: Distinguish gene ancestry from population separation
slides.html: Sampled gene copies can share ancestry before the populations containing them became separated. Their molecular history need not mark the population split exactly. This is another reason one short sequence should not be treated as a complete historical clock for an entire species. Multiple markers, appropriate sampling and comparison with independent fossil evidence can help assess the interpretation without eliminating every uncertainty.

slides.title: Appropriate course emphasis
slides.html: Molecular-clock examples are useful supporting applications of biochemical comparison and quantitative reasoning. They should teach unit handling, assumptions and evidence limits, not imply that SCSA requires advanced dating software or a universal rate to memorise. A defensible answer states the supplied model, shows the calculation, gives the unit and qualifies the estimate according to the information actually available in the question.

This is one reason raw endpoint differences can underestimate substitution history, particularly over long divergences, and why models and independent evidence matter.

title: Evolution of Genes
objectives: Explain gene duplication and divergence.
Distinguish gene histories from organismal histories.
Evaluate conflicting molecular, anatomical and fossil evidence.

glossary.definition: Production of an additional copy of a gene or genomic region.
A group of related genes descended from ancestral copies.
Movement of genetic material between lineages other than ordinary parent-to-offspring inheritance.

slides.title: Genomes record evolutionary processes
slides.html: Genes change through mutation, duplication, loss and other processes across generations. Comparing related sequences helps reconstruct these histories. A gene’s current function is part of the evidence but not its entire history: related genes can acquire different functions, while unrelated genes can independently contribute to similar functions.

slides.title: Duplication creates additional copies
slides.html: A duplication can produce two related copies where previously there was one. One copy may retain much of the ancestral function while the other accumulates changes, though several outcomes are possible. Copies may partition functions, acquire a new role or become non-functional. Duplication does not automatically produce an advantageous innovation.

diagram.caption: A schematic duplication of a region containing gene B. Segments are not bases, and the diagram does not predict the function or benefit of the extra copy.

slides.title: Gene families retain shared features
slides.html: Related copies that persist and diverge can form a gene family. Globin genes illustrate how related sequences can support different oxygen-related roles or expression patterns. Sequence resemblance and chromosome organisation help investigate their history. A gene family is not evidence that every copy has an identical sequence or is expressed in every tissue.

slides.title: Developmental gene changes can reshape bodies
slides.html: Developmental regulators influence when and where other genes act. Changes in their sequence or regulation can alter body-pattern development. Conserved developmental machinery may be reused in different contexts. Homologous developmental genes do not mean organisms have identical adult anatomy, and not every homologous gene belongs to a developmental regulatory family.

slides.title: Gene and species trees answer different questions
slides.html: A gene tree tracks sampled gene copies; a species tree models lineage relationships among organisms. Duplication and differential loss can make those histories differ. Horizontal transfer can move a gene across lineage boundaries. Before interpreting a gene tree as a species tree, identify which copies were compared and consider plausible alternative histories.

diagram.caption: Different evolutionary events can shape a sampled gene history. Their order and occurrence require evidence; this is not a universal sequence for every gene.

slides.title: Organelles have additional histories
slides.html: Mitochondrial and chloroplast genes provide evidence consistent with bacterial ancestry of those organelles through endosymbiosis. Nuclear and organelle genomes therefore sample different components of cellular history. Comparisons should not assume every gene in a complex cell must share one simple branching path or the same inheritance pattern.

slides.title: Sequence change can obscure relationships
slides.html: Unequal rates, independent similar changes and reversals can complicate molecular inference. A base that changes and later returns to its earlier state leaves no endpoint difference at that position. Rapidly changing lineages can also be incorrectly grouped by some methods. Analytical models and marker choice must address these possibilities.

slides.title: Resolve disagreement by testing evidence
slides.html: Conflicting molecular, anatomical or fossil interpretations call for checking sampling, alignments, homology, dating and analytical assumptions. More independent characters and better methods can distinguish hypotheses. Neither molecular data nor fossils should be declared automatically correct in every conflict. A defensible conclusion states which history is supported, which alternatives remain and why uncertainty persists.

slides.title: A gene family records more than mutation
slides.html: Sequence substitutions alter existing copies, while duplication increases the number of related copies available to subsequent evolution. Over generations, those copies may diverge in sequence and regulation, persist with overlapping functions, or be lost. A family of related genes can therefore preserve evidence of several kinds of historical event. Its present arrangement should not be explained as one mutation inevitably producing a new useful organ.

slides.title: Expression can diverge before function does
slides.html: Two copies may initially encode very similar products yet become active in different tissues or developmental stages. A regulatory difference can change when or where a product is available without immediately changing the product’s amino-acid sequence. Sequence comparison and expression evidence therefore answer complementary questions. A claim of functional divergence needs more support than merely detecting two copies in a genome.

slides.title: Duplication creates possibilities rather than guaranteed progress
What natural selection can preserve
slides.html: If a change in a copy influences phenotype, its effect on reproductive success can affect whether it persists. Some duplications may be harmful, some effectively neutral in a particular context, and others beneficial under relevant conditions. Neither mutation nor duplication anticipates future needs. Describing evolutionary opportunity must be separated from claiming that every additional gene copy was produced for a predetermined purpose.

slides.title: Loss can obscure the earlier family
slides.html: Imagine that an ancestral lineage carried related copies α and β. One descendant retains α and loses β, while another retains β and loses α. A comparison restricted to their surviving genes could misread the sequence divergence as beginning only when the species separated. Wider sampling may reveal the older duplication. Missing copies in incomplete data should also be distinguished from demonstrated evolutionary loss.

slides.title: Different origins require different explanations
slides.html: Most inherited gene relationships in close animal lineages can be studied through ordinary descent, but duplication, loss and other processes can complicate individual histories. Organelle genes also carry evidence of the endosymbiotic origin of their genomic compartment. These possibilities explain why a single simple species diagram cannot automatically serve as the complete history of every gene in a eukaryotic cell.

slides.title: Nuclear and mitochondrial evidence are not interchangeable
Inherited compartments can complement each other
slides.html: Mitochondrial and nuclear sequences can provide useful comparisons, but they sample different inheritance systems and different sets of loci. A mitochondrial result may strongly support a particular inherited lineage while remaining incomplete as an account of overall ancestry. Combining suitable nuclear markers with organelle data can test whether a proposed history is shared broadly or whether different compartments reveal a more complex pattern.

slides.title: An evidence conflict is informative
slides.html: If one marker conflicts with a broader anatomical or molecular interpretation, check whether the same gene copies, organisms and genomic regions were compared. Inspect data quality, alignment and the assumptions used to infer relationships. A conflict does not automatically invalidate an entire category of evidence. It may reveal a genuine gene-specific history or a methodological problem that a better comparison can distinguish.

slides.title: Keep the extension connected to Unit 4
slides.html: The detailed outcomes of gene-family evolution support understanding of molecular evidence and bioinformatics. The central examinable link is that improved genetic comparisons can refine evolutionary relationship models. Students should be able to explain why a new dataset changes confidence in a relationship and identify an appropriate limitation. Memorising elaborate gene-family histories is less useful than interpreting the supplied evidence accurately and cautiously.

A gene family can therefore record duplication and divergence, but the survival and effects of particular copies depend on their biological context and evolutionary history.

questions.prompt: Explain why organelle sequences and nuclear sequences should not automatically be treated as independent samples of exactly the same inheritance history.
questions.model: Organelle genomes and nuclear genomes differ in origin and often in inheritance patterns. Mitochondrial and chloroplast sequences carry evidence of endosymbiotic bacterial ancestry, while a nuclear genome has its own recombination and gene-copy histories. Agreement can be informative, but disagreement may reflect biological history or analysis rather than simple error. A sound interpretation states which genomic compartment and inheritance model the evidence represents.

title: Cladistics
objectives: Identify clades and sister groups using branching order.
Distinguish shared derived traits from broadly ancestral traits.
Explain why branch rotation and branch length must be interpreted carefully.

glossary.definition: A common ancestor and all its descendants.
Two lineages that share an immediate common ancestral node.
A character state inherited from a particular common ancestor that helps identify a group.
A hypothesis of branching relationships; branch length does not imply time unless a scale is specified.

slides.title: A clade includes every descendant
slides.html: Cladistics groups organisms by common ancestry. A clade includes an ancestral lineage and all descendants of that ancestor. It is therefore monophyletic. Choosing a group because its members look alike can exclude some descendants or combine unrelated lineages, so appearance alone does not guarantee that a selected group is a clade.

slides.title: Nodes represent common ancestry
slides.html: At a branching node, descendant lineages trace back to a shared ancestor. Sister groups share an immediate ancestral node with each other. Tip position does not show that one living species gave rise to another living species. Modern organisms on different branches have separate histories since their common ancestry.

diagram.caption: A and B are sister groups; C branches outside their shared clade in this illustrative rooted tree. No living tip is shown as the direct ancestor of another tip.

slides.title: Use shared derived characters
slides.html: A shared derived character helps identify descendants of a particular ancestor relative to the comparison being made. A broadly ancestral character may occur in several groups and fail to distinguish a smaller clade. For example, a vertebral column does not by itself distinguish one primate group from another because it is shared much more widely.

slides.title: Character choice affects the hypothesis
slides.html: Morphological analyses compare anatomical characters; molecular analyses compare appropriate genetic or protein characters. Homology should be assessed because convergence can produce superficially similar states. A tree should use an informative collection of characters rather than assuming that one feature or one untested resemblance always determines the complete relationship.

slides.title: Nested groups are compatible
slides.html: Clades can sit inside larger clades. A lineage may therefore belong to several nested ancestry-based groups without contradiction. A paraphyletic selection includes an ancestor but omits some descendants. A polyphyletic grouping brings together lineages while excluding their relevant common ancestry, often because a similarity evolved independently.

diagram.caption: Group membership depends on ancestry and descendant inclusion, not on the shape of a drawn outline.

slides.title: Rotate branches without changing ancestry
slides.html: Branches can rotate around a node while preserving their connections. Thus the same relationships can appear in different left-to-right orders. Read the nodes rather than counting how close two tips look on the page. Rotating a branch is not the same as moving a lineage to a different ancestral node.

slides.title: Branch length needs an explicit scale
slides.html: A basic cladogram represents branching order without an automatic time scale. In a time-scaled tree, branch positions or lengths may represent elapsed time; in another molecular tree they may represent estimated sequence change. Check the legend. A visually longer branch does not automatically mean an older, superior or more advanced living species.

slides.title: Construct and test a hypothesis
slides.html: A simple analysis lists taxa, identifies comparable character states and uses an outgroup to help distinguish ancestral from derived states. Candidate branching arrangements are then evaluated against the data. Missing information, homoplasy and conflicting signals can support alternatives. A cladogram is a testable relationship hypothesis, not a permanent ranking of organisms from primitive to advanced.

slides.title: Find the root and trace connections
slides.html: Before interpreting a supplied tree, identify the root if it is shown and follow each relevant tip back towards shared nodes. The node where two paths first meet is their most recent common ancestor in that model. Compare that node with the ancestor shared with a third lineage. This connection-based reading is more reliable than counting centimetres between names at the tips.

slides.title: Work through a three-taxon example
slides.html: Suppose A and B meet at one node, and their combined branch joins C at a deeper node. A and B are sister groups; each shares the same more recent common ancestor with the other than with C. Rotating the A–B node swaps their displayed positions but preserves that relationship. No rearrangement of the page order alone turns modern A into the ancestor of modern B.

slides.title: Two drawings of the same branching connections
A clade is defined by descent
slides.html: On a supplied branching tree, selecting a node and all descendant lineages identifies a clade. Leaving out one descendant changes the selected set even if the remaining members look similar. This is why a group based only on present appearance can fail to match ancestry. A distinctive feature may support a clade, but the group’s definition follows common descent rather than a popularity ranking of characteristics.

slides.title: Characters depend on the comparison
slides.html: A trait inherited from a remote ancestor can unite a broad group yet fail to distinguish a smaller one. For example, having a vertebral column does not resolve relationships among great apes because all possess it. A derived state is informative relative to a particular ancestral comparison. The terms ancestral and derived do not label organisms as inferior or superior, and they can change with the scale of comparison.

slides.title: An absent time scale limits conclusions
slides.html: An unscaled cladogram shows the branching connections proposed by the model. It does not automatically date the shared ancestors or measure how much molecular change occurred. A long drawn branch can simply reflect page layout. If time or change is encoded, the diagram must state the scale. Read that legend before making any claim about age, rate or evolutionary distance.

slides.title: Nested classification does not mean modern ancestors
Sampled fossils need cautious placement
slides.html: A fossil assigned near a branch can provide evidence about traits and the existence of related lineages, but its placement may be uncertain because material is incomplete. A labelled fossil tip is not automatically the direct ancestor of every nearby living tip. A defensible interpretation distinguishes a proposed relationship from a demonstrated parent–descendant connection and considers whether additional fossils could change the model.

slides.title: Molecular evidence can refine a tree
slides.html: A new, appropriately sampled sequence comparison may support an existing grouping, resolve a previously uncertain branch or conflict with a prior interpretation. Researchers assess which model best explains the combined evidence and its limitations. Refinement is part of scientific reasoning, not evidence that relationships are arbitrary. The explanation should state which new observations support the revised connection rather than simply appealing to newer technology.

slides.title: Interpretation is the syllabus priority
slides.html: SCSA requires interpretation of evolutionary relationships using supplied phylogenetic trees, while construction of those trees is not required. Practice should therefore emphasise common ancestors, sister groups, nested membership, branch rotation and appropriate reading of scales. Creating a tree may be an optional supporting activity, but students should not be told that mastering a particular construction algorithm is necessary Unit 4 examination content.

questions.prompt: Which set is a clade?
options: A common ancestor and only the descendants that look similar
All large-bodied species regardless of ancestry
A common ancestor and all its descendants
Any two tips drawn next to one another
feedback: Omitting descendants can make a selection paraphyletic.
Body size alone does not establish a single ancestry-based clade.
Correct. A clade is a complete monophyletic group.
Visual proximity is not sufficient; branching connections determine ancestry.

questions.prompt: A branch is rotated around its node without changing any connections. What happens?
options: The evolutionary relationships remain the same
The species instantly becomes more advanced
The oldest tip must now be the youngest
The common ancestor disappears
feedback: Correct. Rotation changes the drawing’s order, not its branching topology.
A drawing change does not alter evolution or establish progress.
Tip age is not determined by left-to-right placement.
The node and its ancestry remain part of the same topology.

questions.prompt: In an unscaled cladogram, what does a longer drawn branch necessarily show?
options: More years since divergence
A higher mutation rate
Greater evolutionary superiority
Nothing quantitative about time unless a relevant scale is supplied
feedback: Time requires an explicit interpretation or scale.
A line drawn longer is not automatically a measured substitution rate.
Evolutionary trees do not rank living organisms as superior.
Correct. Basic branching diagrams encode relationships rather than automatic quantitative time.

questions.prompt: Why might possession of a backbone be unhelpful for distinguishing two closely related primate groups?
options: It is unique to only one primate species
It is a widely shared ancestral feature in this comparison
It cannot ever be inherited
It is a DNA laboratory artefact
feedback: Backbones occur in a much wider vertebrate group.
Correct. A broadly ancestral state may not identify the smaller branching distinction.
An anatomical state can be inherited through developmental mechanisms.
A backbone is an anatomical feature, not a laboratory artefact.
questions.explanation: Correct. A broadly ancestral state may not identify the smaller branching distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would decide whether two taxa are more closely related on a cladogram without relying on their positions on the page.
questions.model: Trace their branches towards the root and identify their most recent common ancestor. Compare that node with the common ancestral nodes they share with other taxa. A more recent shared node indicates a closer relationship in the tree. Left-to-right tip order and visual distance are unreliable because branches can be rotated around nodes without altering the branching connections.
criteria: Identify the most recent common ancestral node.
Compare the relevant branching connections.
Reject visual tip order or distance as the criterion.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a shared derived character from a shared ancestral character and explain why the distinction depends on the comparison.
questions.model: A shared derived state identifies a change inherited from a particular common ancestor relative to the lineages being compared. An ancestral state was already present before that smaller group arose and may be shared much more widely. For example, a vertebral column supports a broad vertebrate grouping but does not separate two primate lineages. The character’s usefulness therefore depends on which taxa and ancestral reference are considered.
criteria: Define derived and ancestral states relative to a comparison.
Use an appropriate example.
Explain why a broadly shared trait may not resolve a smaller clade.
